consensus_summary: Biblical peace primarily means shalom as comprehensive wholeness and right relationship/reconciliation with God accomplished through Christ, a divine gift rather than mere absence of conflict; complementary facets include inner calm, social peacemaking, eschatological harmony, and warnings against false peace.
book_summary: Peace is the covenant made whole (shalom from root complete/restore/repay): the work of righteousness and the great peace of those who love the law; not the world’s truce or a feeling, but the restored peace the gospel publishes, opposed to the counterfeit “peace, peace” over an unkept covenant.
consensus_core_identification: Shalom as Christ-accomplished reconciliation and restored right relationship/wholeness with God.
book_core_identification: Shalom as the covenant made whole (complete/restore), identified as the work of righteousness and the peace of law-lovers, published by the gospel.
boundary_disagreement: Book definitionally conditions peace on the work of righteousness and love of the law while categorically excluding subjective feeling; consensus primary centers objective peace via justification by faith (not law-conditioned) and admits inward calm as a common complementary facet.
material_contradiction: None; both identify the same restored-shalom/covenant referent distinct from worldly truce, mere feeling, or counterfeit peace.
rationale: Minimum cores share the same central referent of restored shalom/covenant wholeness (not world/truce/feeling/false peace) published or realized in the gospel. The book preserves this category but materially narrows precision, conditions, and extension by making “work of righteousness” and “love the law” definitional and by framing the whole as covenant completion, thereby excluding or reclassifying some cases (pure feeling-as-peace; faith-reconciliation detached from law-righteousness framing) that broader consensus admits as primary or complementary. Extra verse detail and emphasis do not replace the referent.
strongest_objection: Elevating “work of righteousness” and “love the law” as definitional risks sidelining the consensus NT center that peace with God is received by faith apart from works of the law (e.g., Rom 5:1), shifting the soteriological condition.
